articles.desc: The miss was too small to shift the policy outlook. Markets still price an October 28 hike as near certain and a cumulative 50 basis points of tightening by the end of February. The kiwi’s dip just below 0.57 suggests traders trimmed only the most aggressive hike bets. Oil is the key swing factor fr
articles.content: The miss was too small to shift the policy outlook. Markets still price an October 28 hike as near certain and a cumulative 50 basis points of tightening by the end of February. The kiwi’s dip just below 0.57 suggests traders trimmed only the most aggressive hike bets. Oil is the key swing factor from here: the Middle East war is lifting fuel, fertiliser and transport costs, and with petrol already the biggest contributor to inflation, any further rise in crude feeds directly into the expected fourth-quarter rebound. That keeps the risk skewed toward a longer tightening cycle. NZD support is likely to depend on how hawkish the RBNZ’s guidance proves next week rather than on today’s data. - Earlier: New Zealand Q3 CPI 3.7% y/y (expected 3.8%, prior 4.1%) - New Zealand’s inflation undershot forecasts, but with core pressures firm and fuel prices climbing again, the miss looks more like a pause in the problem than a turn in it. Summary: Annual CPI slowed to 3.7% in the third quarter from 4.1%, below the 3.8% Reuters poll forecast and the RBNZ’s 3.9% projection Quarterly CPI rose 0.7%, against expectations of 0.8% Petrol was the largest contributor to inflation despite easing from the June quarter; house-building costs also rose Non-tradeable inflation eased to 3.3% from 3.4%, while tradeable inflation was 4.3% Markets price a 98% chance of a hike next week and a full 50 basis points of tightening by the end of February; the NZD dipped to around 0.569 Economists expect inflation to rebound in the fourth quarter, with ASB forecasting 4.5% by year-end New Zealand’s annual inflation slowed to 3.7% in the third quarter, below economists’ forecasts but still above the top of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s target range, official data showed on Thursday. The result did little to shift expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates next week. The consumer price index rose 0.7% from the second quarter, Statistics New Zealand said, compared with a 0.8% increase expected by economists polled by Reuters. The annual rate eased from 4.1% in the June quarter and came in below both the 3.8% consensus and the RBNZ’s own 3.9% projection. The central bank targets annual inflation of 1% to 3% over the medium term. Statistics New Zealand said petrol prices were the largest contributor to inflation, even though they had eased from the June quarter, and that house-building costs had also risen. Non-tradeable inflation, which captures domestically driven price pressures, eased to 3.3% from 3.4%. Tradeable inflation, which covers imported goods including fuel, was 4.3%. The New Zealand dollar dipped to around 0.569 against the US dollar after the release. However, markets continue to price a 98% chance of a rate hike at next week’s monetary policy review, and fully price 50 basis points of tightening by the end of February. The RBNZ has raised the official cash rate twice this year to 2.75%. Westpac New Zealand senior economist Satish Ranchhod said that although the result was below the RBNZ’s forecast, firm core inflation would give policymakers pause for thought. He said a hike next week now looked like the path of least resistance, with market pricing and economist views converging on a move. Economists expect inflation to pick up again in the fourth quarter as fuel prices rise once more. ASB forecasts inflation of 4.5% by year-end and said its 2027 profile looks considerably firmer than the RBNZ’s September projections. The Middle East war is adding to stagflation risks globally by disrupting energy supplies and shipping, which is lifting fuel, fertiliser and transport costs. The data is the last major release before the RBNZ’s decision. It lands as inflation becomes a central issue ahead of the closely contested November 7 general election. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Bridge repairs delayed as businesses suffer
articles.desc: A CENTRAL Andros businesswoman says the closure of the Fresh Creek Bridge forced her to shut down her business last month, and she now spends her days waiting for any work that comes her way.
articles.content: Bridge repairs delayed as businesses suffer | The Tribune Bridge repairs delayed as businesses suffer The Condemned Fresh Creek Bridge in Andros. A CENTRAL Andros businesswoman says the closure of the Fresh Creek Bridge forced her to shut down her business last month, and she now spends her days waiting for any work that comes her way. “I just sit and pray that somebody call me that they need something,” Hanna Mott told The Tribune yesterday. Ms Mott, who runs Diamond Wheels on Wheels and sells food at the roadside, said trade slowed so much after the bridge closed that she had to put everything on hold. She is now trying to sell soft drinks and food from her home while looking for other work in the community. “I put everything on hold because of the bridge, people can’t come over with their cars,” she said. “You can’t hardly go shopping and nothing like that it doesn’t make sense.” She said businesses in the area had lost at least 50 percent of their profits because customers could no longer easily reach them. “A lot of people over here lost a lot,” she said. Ms Mott said she had seen a local school principal walking students halfway across the bridge so they could get home, and that some children were left disappointed after missing the school’s fun day because they could not get across. With cars barred from the bridge, residents have been parking near one end, walking to the other side and trying to find rides from there. Ms Mott said there is no reliable ferry between the northern and southern sides of Central Andros. One ferry ran for about a month before stopping, she said, and another began earlier this week but left after a single day. Ms Mott, who lives in Davis Creek and has run her business for about two years, said the settlement had also suffered power outages, poor telephone service and limited transport in recent months. She criticised the government’s response and called on Central, Mangrove Cay and South Andros MP Leon Lundy to make sure the bridge is properly repaired rather than patched up. Her frustration was echoed yesterday outside the Office of the Prime Minister by Progressive Liberal Party supporter Edison McKenzie, who accused Mr Lundy of wanting to put a “band-aid” on the bridge instead of fixing it properly. “The people in Central Andros are fed up, and we will not accept no patching up on no bridge anymore,” he told reporters. Mr McKenzie said Mr Lundy had assured residents that repairs were under way. He also claimed several residents had been hurt because of the bridge’s condition, recalling an incident in which a man’s foot went through the bridge, leaving him needing about 30 stitches. Minister of Works and Family Island Affairs Clay Sweeting told reporters that a structural component needed to support the bridge had arrived in the country, and that the contractor would carry out the repairs when the weather allowed. The Fresh Creek Bridge, which links Andros Town and Coakley Town, was condemned in August after engineers found that a structural support had sunk. The sinking shifted the bridge’s weight onto other supports and caused three sections to drop by about nine inches. Officials first planned a temporary bridge to keep vehicles moving while a permanent replacement was designed. The government dropped the idea after contractors estimated it would cost more than $10m. Mr Sweeting said at the time that the cost “wasn’t feasible to the ministry”. In September, the government said it would instead spend about $400,000 repairing the existing bridge, with work expected to begin on October 1 and take four to six weeks. The repaired bridge is meant to serve in the interim while the government tenders for a permanent replacement. Concerns about the more than 50-year-old bridge are not new. In 2020, it was closed after a mailboat struck it. In 2023, officials acknowledged it was in poor condition, as residents raised concerns about its safety and design. articles.title: 401(k) now rivals healthcare as top employee benefit, but sponsors can’t close the usage gap
articles.desc: A Morgan Stanley survey of 200 plan sponsors finds understanding the plan has become their single biggest concern
articles.content: 401(k) now rivals healthcare as top employee benefit, but sponsors can’t close the usage gap | Insurance Business 401(k) now rivals healthcare as top employee benefit, but sponsors can’t close the usage gap A Morgan Stanley survey of 200 plan sponsors finds understanding the plan has become their single biggest concern The 401(k) plan has officially pulled even with healthcare as the benefit employees value most, according to Morgan Stanley’s . That elevation, however, is creating a new problem for the organizations that sponsor them. Survey respondents now rank helping employees understand the plan as their top concern, cited by 45% as one of their top three worries, up from 32% in 2024. That shift from competing to communicating captures something significant about where plan sponsors are right now: they’ve won the battle for perceived importance and are losing the one for actual engagement. Thirty-four percent of the 200 plan sponsors surveyed said employees now rank the defined contribution plan as their single most valued benefit, more than double the 15% who said the same in 2024. The survey polled investment decision-makers at organizations with at least $50 million in plan assets; more than two-thirds represented plans over $250 million. The shift, the report suggests, reflects workers in peak earning years with thinning defined benefit pension options and Social Security uncertainty treating their 401(k) account as a primary household asset rather than one workplace perk among many. Elevated status and actual usage are not the same thing, and the survey’s data makes that gap visible. When sponsors that offer managed accounts were asked what percentage of participants use the feature, the average answer was 12%. Among sponsors not offering managed accounts and not planning to add them, the dominant objections were high participant fees, cited by 64%, and insufficient perceived value, cited by 56%. The pattern is consistent in retirement income. Eighty-six percent of respondents said offering retirement income solutions is important or critical, but fiduciary concerns have since 2024 overtaken lack of participant understanding as the leading barrier to implementation, cited by 63%. The finding suggests the SECURE 2.0’s momentum on retirement income adoption may be slowing as liability questions reassert themselves, rather than accelerating as the regulatory landscape settles. That combination of high aspiration and low adoption is the specific terrain on which benefits advisors operate. Sponsors cite investment advisors and consultants as their most valuable resource in assessing their plan lineup, ranked among the top three by 69% of respondents. The same sponsors identify comprehension and engagement as their top unresolved concern. The two things are connected: the advisor relationship is the channel through which education strategy and plan design decisions actually get made, and the survey signals that sponsors are ready to be pushed on both. Where advisors are being asked to do more The participant engagement section of the survey offers the most granular picture of what sponsors say they need. When asked in open-ended questions what tools would most effectively drive higher participant engagement, sponsors coalesced around four themes: group education sessions, personalized one-on-one consultations (virtual or in-person), content tailored by demographic or life stage, and broader financial wellness topics beyond retirement. These are not product requests. They are design and delivery requests. The kind that advisors are positioned to help structure and execute. The 3(38) versus 3(21) data adds a useful advisory-model layer. Only 26% of surveyed sponsors use a discretionary 3(38) investment manager, compared with 56% using a non-discretionary 3(21) advisor. articles.desc: Says concessions to Washington could hurt soybean and dairy producers, squeeze rural incomes and hasten corporate consolidation
articles.content: All India Kisan Sabha warns of 'militant resistance' if US trade deal proceeds All India Kisan Sabha warns of 'militant resistance' if US trade deal proceeds Says concessions to Washington could hurt soybean and dairy producers, squeeze rural incomes and hasten corporate consolidation Twitter X Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.com Twitter X Streamline Icon: https://streamlinehq.com AIKS warns of 'militant resistance' if the Modi government proceeds with the proposed India-US trade deal. Farmers' body flags risks to soybean, dairy, cotton, feed-crop and fruit producers from US imports. AIKS criticises edible oil duty cuts and backs the Samyukt Kisan Morcha's 23 October Delhi march. The All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS) on Wednesday, 21 October warned the Narendra Modi government of 'militant resistance' from farmers if it proceeds with the proposed India-US trade deal, arguing that concessions to Washington would threaten domestic agriculture and strengthen corporate control over the sector. In a statement, the farmers' organisation urged the government to reject the proposed agreement, saying Indian farmers would be unable to compete with heavily subsidised American agricultural producers. Describing the proposed deal as a surrender to US interests, the AIKS warned that the government would 'face militant resistance from the peasantry if it goes ahead with the anti-national trade deal'. It also called on its units to prepare for a prolonged struggle against the agreement. 'The ongoing visit of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and the negotiations he reportedly led with Indian authorities to "finalise" a trade deal between the US and India, demonstrate that the RSS-BJP-led Union government will go to any extent to please their imperial masters,' the AIKS said. The organisation alleged that Parliament had been kept in the dark about the proposed agreement even as negotiations appeared to be nearing completion. Citing public remarks by Rubio that the deal was 'very close', the AIKS said access for US dairy products to the Indian market had emerged as the final hurdle. It also referred to Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal's statement that the agreement had reached the final stage of legal drafting. US lawmakers call on Trump to press Xi on soybean, beef trade issue Soybean and dairy sectors at risk, says AIKS The AIKS warned that concessions in the soybean sector could severely affect farmers in major producing states, including Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Karnataka. 'Indian soybean farmers cannot compete with heavily subsidised industrial farmers in the US,' it said. The organisation also cautioned against opening India's dairy market without limits, arguing that cheaper, subsidised imports could undercut domestic procurement prices and threaten the livelihoods and household incomes of dairy farmers. Other sectors that could be affected include maize and sorghum growers supplying cattle feed, cotton farmers, and producers of almonds, walnuts and apples, the AIKS said. 'To put it simply, concessions to the US would result in a dangerous level of corporate consolidation in Indian agriculture,' it added. AIKS criticises cuts in edible oil import duties The farmers' body also criticised the government's decision in September to reduce the basic import duty on crude soybean oil and palm oil from 10 per cent to 5 per cent, alongside cuts in duties on refined oils. It said the decision came just as farmers were beginning to harvest kharif soybeans, potentially exposing domestic producers to greater competition from imported edible oils at a critical point in the agricultural cycle. The AIKS argued that such trade and tariff decisions could weaken returns for domestic farmers while benefiting large importers and corporate players. articles.title: Jackdaw exposes the muddle of Labour’s economic thinking
articles.content: Jackdaw exposes the muddle of Labour’s economic thinking Lord Frost led the negotiations that finally took Britain out of the EU in 2020. A Cabinet minister in the Boris Johnson government, he resigned in protest at the handling of Covid lockdowns, and has since been a persistent advocate of a more fully conservative approach to policy on the Right. He is a non-affiliated peer in the House of Lords. Even a stopped clock is right twice a day. And every so often even this Labour government gets something right. The approval of the Jackdaw North Sea gas field is one such moment. Of course, it is to be welcomed. But enabling Britain to use its own gas really ought to be the ordinary business of government, not an occasion for national rejoicing. After all, it has taken 20 years to get to this point. . Rishi Sunak’s government licensed it, only to be blocked by the courts. Now finally we have definitive approval. Gas will flow before the end of the year. At last. Jackdaw is not a panacea. The Government expects it to increase domestic gas production by around 6 per cent at its peak, with a lifespan of up to 11 years. That is about 2 per cent of UK demand. There may not be a huge impact on prices, but that is not the point. The case for Jackdaw is that we should use our own oil and gas, not other people’s. Domestic production supports jobs, tax revenues and security of supply. It has downstream effects on the wider British economy that buying Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) from Qatar or the US, still less wind turbines or solar panels from China, simply do not have. The green case against all this amounts to saying that producing things in Britain is pointless unless doing so helps determine the world price. Follow that logic and Britain wouldn’t make anything much – a nation of spectators, buying in everything and producing nothing. It is true, of course, that Jackdaw only supports a couple of dozen jobs directly. But once again that is the point. Producing a lot of something we want with only a few jobs and no government subsidy is a good thing. We get lots of gas, and everyone else can go and do something else that also adds to the national wealth. That increase in productivity is why we aren’t all still tilling the fields. Jobs are a cost, not a benefit. The much-vaunted tens of thousands of “green jobs” in the heavily subsidised “net zero economy” represent a move from a productive to a less productive energy system. They are therefore not part of the solution but part of the problem. That’s why what matters is not so much the Jackdaw decision, which was a no-brainer in current circumstances, but whether that decision represents a new trajectory. On that, one must be unconvinced. Yes, it’s obvious that the Starmer government and Ed Miliband, in particular, did not want to license Jackdaw Andy Burnham’s Government, more in touch with the unions, not just Labour “progressives”, read the room better. But what happens next? After all, they could have too. They didn’t. If it’s approved in future, they will get another day of criticism from the cranky green Left that they could have avoided. So one must be suspicious. One look at the stony faces on the benches behind Burnham told you everything about Labour’s real level of enthusiasm. The real charge against ministers on the back of the decision is not that they have abandoned their policy. It is that they have not. Even now, the Government is announcing a designed to channel North Sea tax revenues into renewable and low-carbon projects. That’s one signal that there will be no letting up on the subsidised move to renewables. And here’s another. Burnham described the Jackdaw decision as a “bridge to the future”. Unite’s Sharon Graham is giving the Government a bit of cover for this, presenting it as buying time to support investment in industries like “wind turbine manufacture and refining green jet fuel”. Call me sceptical about whether we can build a windmill industry at Chinese expens

The 2026 NIC Fall Conference – being held at the Sheraton Grand Chicago Riverwalk – brings senior housing leaders together to turn opportunity into action through meaningful industry connections, strategic learning and informed decision-making. Focused on the relationships and insights that drive business forward, the conference provides a forum for industry leaders to explore emerging opportunities and help shape the future of senior housing. The session will take place Thursday, October 22, from 4 to 5 p.m. Schuerer will join fellow panelists Renee Kimberly, Vice President of Sales, Strategy & Enablement at Senior Lifestyle, and Kristen Paris, Vice President of Market Research at ProMatura. Andrew Smith, Senior Vice President of Healthspan and Innovation at HumanGood, will moderate the discussion. As prospective residents and families increasingly turn to AI platforms such as ChatGPT and Gemini to research senior living options, organizations face a new strategic challenge: understanding what these tools say about their communities and how those answers influence consumer perceptions and decisions before a prospect ever makes contact. “AI is fundamentally changing how prospective residents and their families discover, evaluate and select senior living communities,” said Schuerer. “For executives, this is a strategic imperative not simply a marketing challenge. Organizations must ensure their brands are differentiated, their value proposition is clear and their digital content establishes credibility to influence how AI interprets their expertise and recommends their communities.” The session will feature live demonstrations and hands-on searches designed to help attendees see how AI platforms represent their communities using publicly available information, online reviews and digital content. Panelists will share practical approaches to identifying inaccurate information, strengthening brand visibility in AI-generated answers and translating AI-driven interest into meaningful leads. Schuerer brings a strategic perspective at the intersection of communications, brand strategy, digital marketing and consumer experience. In his role with Franciscan Ministries and Franciscan Advisory Services, he leads initiatives designed to strengthen brand differentiation, enhance digital engagement and support growth. (Jeremy Wadsworth/The Blade via AP) cms.site.custom.site_domain : therecord.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/waterloo_region_record WINDSOR - A spokesperson for the mayor of Windsor, Ont., says the border city is monitoring a toxic chemical leak in Toledo, Ohio that prompted evacuations on Tuesday night. The spokesperson says the risk to Windsor residents is “very low” as the city is about 90 kilometres northeast of Toledo on the shores of Lake Erie and winds are blowing in the opposite direction. Hundreds of Toledo residents fled their homes and sheltered in place Tuesday night after a chemical tank exploded, raising fears of an ongoing glycidyl methacrylate leak. The industrial chemical can burn the eyes, nose, mouth and skin and is toxic if ingested, according to local officials in Ohio. Toledo Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz says a police officer was injured while responding to the tank explosion and there’s concern the tank could explode again. He says officials don’t know what caused the explosion. Director of the Toledo-Lucas County Health Department Karim Baroudi is advising Toledo residents to close their windows as officials work to determine the level of toxicity in the air. The city ordered people within a 1.6-kilometre radius of the explosion to evacuate their homes and businesses Tuesday night. A shelter-in-place order was issued for residents beyond the evacuation zone within a 4.8-kilometre radius. The Canadian Press has reached out to federal and Ontario environment ministries for comment but did not immediately hear back. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026. articles.title: IIT Madras launches UDYOG programme for biotech industry skill development
articles.desc: The UDYOG programme combines online courses, intensive laboratory training, pilot-scale exposure and opportunities for industry internships.
articles.content: IIT Madras launches UDYOG programme for biotech industry skill development - The HinduBusinessLine Core sector grew at 7.9% in September; industrial outlook remains uncertain Sugar-ethanol curbs put auto industry’s E20 transition to test; OMCs face ₹813-crore potential cost increase Commerce Department steps up FTA outreach amid low utilisation Sundaram MF enters SIF business with launch of Select Equity Ex-Top 100 Long Short Fund ICICI Lombard bets on disciplined risk selection for profitable growth: CFO IIT Madras launches UDYOG programme for biotech industry skill development The UDYOG programme combines online courses, intensive laboratory training, pilot-scale exposure and opportunities for industry internships. https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/education/iit-madras-launches-udyog-programme-for-biotech-industry-skill-development/article71607197.ece V Kamakoti, Director, IIT Madras, inaugurated UDYOG, an industry-oriented finishing school to equip young graduates with practical skills and professional competencies required by the biotechnology and biomanufacturing sectors, in Chennai on Wednesday. The Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT Madras) has launched UDYOG, an industry-oriented finishing school to equip young graduates with practical skills and professional competencies required by the biotechnology and biomanufacturing sectors. UDYOG (Upskilling and Development for Young Graduates) aims to bridge the gap between academic education and industry requirements through a structured training pathway. It combines online courses, intensive laboratory training, pilot-scale exposure and opportunities for industry internships. The first batch of the Finishing School is scheduled to commence on January 18, 2027, and the early-bird registration closes on December 15, 2026. Launched through SynBioME, the IIT Madras-TICEL Biofoundry, the programme is focussed on advancing biotechnology research, and is intended for pre-final-year and final-year students pursuing B.Tech., M.Tech. and M.Sc. degrees in biotechnology and allied disciplines, across all colleges and institutes in India. V Kamakoti, Director, IIT Madras, inaugurated the programme here on Wednessday. “AI also means Academia-Industry. It is becoming an absolute necessity that every discipline of Science and Engineering must look at this AI with care to make themselves relevant to the modern world. The leaked details reportedly include names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, gender, email IDs, residential addresses, bank branches, Customer Information File (CIF) details, Lead IDs and loan-related records. SBI said it received information about the exposure from the Defence Cyber Agency and CERT-In on October 16 and is investigating the extent of the data theft. SBI has stated that all banking services are functioning normally and that immediate measures have been taken to address the incident. The bank has not named any hacker group in its stock exchange filing, while the group called Sirisym reportedly claimed access to data belonging to around 3.75 lakh customers. Cybersecurity experts advise customers to use unique passwords, activate transaction alerts and two-factor authentication, avoid suspicious links, check credit reports and lock Aadhaar biometrics. The dark web is also used for illegal trading of stolen data, making vigilance essential. articles.title: Hephaestus Technologies: Hephaestus Exits Stealth Having Raised $17.2M to Supply Rare-Earth-Free HTS Superconductors and Build Low-Cost Fusion Power
articles.desc: CiRi Ventures leads latest funding round as novel HTS magnets head to manufacturing in 2027, ahead of a negative triangularity reactor targeting net energy gain by 2030 Hephaestus today emerged fr...
articles.content: Hephaestus Technologies: Hephaestus Exits Stealth Having Raised $17.2M to Supply Rare-Earth-Free HTS Superconductors and Build Low-Cost Fusion Power Hephaestus Technologies: Hephaestus Exits Stealth Having Raised $17.2M to Supply Rare-Earth-Free HTS Superconductors and Build Low-Cost Fusion Power Hephaestus Technologies: Hephaestus Exits Stealth Having Raised $17.2M to Supply Rare-Earth-Free HTS Superconductors and Build Low-Cost Fusion Power CiRi Ventures leads latest funding round as novel HTS magnets head to manufacturing in 2027, ahead of a negative triangularity reactor targeting net energy gain by 2030 Hephaestus today emerged from stealth with solutions that address two of the largest cost drivers in fusion power: the high temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets that confine the plasma, and the edge-localized modes (ELMs major plasma instabilities) that drive up the cost and complexity of conventional reactor designs. The company also announced the close of a new funding round led by CiRi Ventures. Hephaestus was founded in London in 2019 with a single mission to help make fusion energy cheap enough to compete on the grid. Its AI plasma solver initially swept the full space of tokamak design parameters, unconstrained by the legacy designs and materials much of the industry is already committed to, and identified negative triangularity (NT), which inverts the D-shaped plasma used in most tokamaks, as the most likely configuration for low-cost fusion energy. Subsequent results from facilities worldwide, including the DIII-D, JET, and SMART, have shown that NT can deliver strong performance without ELM instabilities. In February 2021, Antoine Pochelon joined as co-founder and Head of the Experimental Campaign. Dr. Pochelon spent decades at EPFL, producing many of negative triangularity's foundational experimental results, and is among the field's leading authorities on NT physics. The company has already moved into hardware. Its first device, Anvil 0, the world's first tokamak designed for NT from inception, was completed in 2024. Hephaestus has applied the same AI-first approach to fusion's largest capital cost and biggest bottleneck to scale: the HTS magnets that confine the plasma. Using its proprietary AI materials discovery platform, MaDi-AI, the company has identified, manufactured, and characterized at lab scale multiple novel HTS materials, validated by the UK's National Physical Laboratory. Every HTS magnet in fusion today is made from REBCO (rare-earth barium copper oxide), a superconductor whose manufacture is slow, expensive to scale, and concentrated in regions of geopolitical risk. Hephaestus is developing rare-earth-free HTS materials that are more affordable, more scalable and far less exposed to geostrategic bottlenecks than REBCO, positioning the company as a foundational supplier to the wider fusion sector as well as a fusion energy provider in its own right. The new funding will accelerate two critical milestones: HTS manufacturing at its new 70,000 ft New Jersey facility starting in 2027 and, by 2030, a demonstration of NT's commercial advantages in a net gain demonstration reactor (Q>1). Existing investors include Prescience Ventures, Teampact Ventures, Climate Capital, Unruly Capital, and CiRi Ventures. "Fusion has the potential of adding tens of GW's per year of clean stable power to the grid, but that only happens if it becomes affordable and scalable," said Jack Zamattio, CEO and founder of Hephaestus. "That's why we chose negative triangularity, and why we're manufacturing our own novel HTS magnets, to realise fusion's full industrial potential." Hephaestus has already opened early-access discussions with fusion developers seeking HTS supply, and is actively hiring across its New Jersey, London, and Rome sites. articles.title: New digital archive aims to save Scotland's deteriorating castles
articles.desc: The Scottish Castles Association and the University of Stirling are developing a digital archive to record Scotland’s castles, preserve historic collections and identify sites at risk.
articles.content: New archive launched to help preserve Scotland's historic castles | The Herald New archive launched to help preserve Scotland's historic castles A colour slide of a photograph of Castle Stalker, Argyll, taken in 1986, from the Peter and Margaret Rourke Collection. (Image: The Scottish Castles Association) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A new online archive aims to document and preserve Scotland’s vanishing castles, creating a digital record of historic sites that are deteriorating or at risk of being lost. The Scottish Castles Association, in partnership with the University of , is developing the archive to record the condition of surviving castles, identify sites at risk and assess opportunities for restoration or adaptive reuse. Comlongon Castle (Alastair Maxwell-Irving Collection) (Image: The Scottish Castles Association) The project, which has been operating on a digital platform, is set to reach a wider audience following a launch event at Dundas Castle. The archive currently includes the Robert and Nicholas Bogdan collection, with further collections being catalogued and digitised. Some material is already available Amisfield Tower (Alastair Maxwell-Irving Collection) (Image: The Scottish Castles Association) The Scottish Castles Association hopes the archive will become a freely accessible resource for anyone interested in Scotland’s castles, bringing together photographs, drawings, research and records previously held across private and institutional collections. It will also establish a baseline for monitoring future changes, helping researchers identify buildings at risk and guide conservation efforts. eBay woodworking plane linked to Royal Mile tradesman sparks public appeal Rare Skibo Castle table suite valued at up to £250,000 heads to auction Glasgow’s Sloans unveils immersive dining experience after £500,000 investment Significant areas of Scotland have not been systematically recorded to modern standards, leaving gaps in knowledge about the condition and risks facing many castles and fortified sites. The archive aims to address these gaps, helping establish which buildings could be saved and ensuring the history and significance of those that cannot be preserved are documented. Slides of Scottish castles from the Peter and Margaret Rourke Collection. (Image: The Scottish Castles Association) The project will also involve local communities, universities, schools and heritage groups. It aims to support a new generation of castle researchers by offering students and volunteers opportunities to develop practical skills in research, photography, photogrammetry and heritage recording. The programme is seeking contributions from supporters who could fund specific elements of the work or help develop the archive as a whole.
